newsitem.title: KENYA: Refugees flee Zaire camp, rebels said to take town.
newsitem.headline: Refugees flee Zaire camp, rebels said to take town.

text.p: Zaire rebels were on Friday reported to have seized the strategic town of Kindu and refugees began to flee the biggest camp in eastern Zaire in fear of a rebel attack.

Michele Quintaglie, a spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme, said: "We have reports that refugee populations have started to move from Tingi Tingi (camp). We have advised our staff to return to Kisangani because of security concerns."
About 170,000 Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi settled at Tingi Tingi after moving westwards to escape the rebel advance that began last October.
"It is confirmed that Kindu and its airport fell to the rebels yesterday (on Thursday)," a U.N. source told Reuters.
He added that all 2,000 Zairean troops in Kindu fled without a fight after extensively looting the town and headed westwards towards the town of Katako-Kombe, 170 km (100 miles) away.
But a Zairean defence ministry official said Kindu remained in army hands on Friday and was reported quiet at midday.
In Rwanda's capital Kigali, Mwenze Kongoro, minister of justice in the rebel administration in east Zaire, told Reuters rebel forces had seized one side of Kindu town and were taking the other.

"We confirm the fall of one side of Kindu. There was no resistance. We were welcomed by the local population. The bridge connecting both sides was mined. We have cleaned those mines and are in the process of taking the other side," he said.

On Tingi Tingi camp, with 170,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees the largest in east Zaire, Kongoro said: "We are six km from Tingi Tingi. We are holding our advance on Tingi Tingi. We are trying to resolve the problem of the refugees."
Tingi Tingi is 260 km (160 miles) northeast of Kindu.
Kongoro said the rebels were concerned about the plight of "innocent men, women and children" among the refugees. "We will eventually take it (Tingi Tingi) but not right now," he added.
Twenty-two foreign aid workers were evacuated on at least three planes from Tingi Tingi in the early afternoon on Friday after they were warned refugees feared an imminent rebel attack.
Aid workers said Zairean troop reinforcements and mercenaries arrived in a rush later on Friday from the city of Kisangani at Tingi Tingi camp backed by warplanes and helicopter gunships.
Kindu, a key, heavily-fortified transport hub on the Zaire River, had the northernmost working station on a rail line to South Africa. It also had a large airport used by the military.

Kindu is 320 km (200 miles) west of the border with Rwanda and is the most westerly town said to fall to the rebels who have seized a stretch of the east more than 1,000 km (600 miles) long since October.
A regional military source told Reuters rebel leader Laurent Kabila returned from exploratory peace talks in South Africa on Friday and headed for his headquarters in the Zairean town of Goma.
Kabila, 56, arrived in South Africa on Tuesday as part of South African attempts to get the two warring sides in face-to -face talks. He met President Nelson Mandela on Wednesday.
In Paris, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said he hoped to persuade member states to reconsider sending a multinational force to eastern Zaire in light of a very serious humanitarian situation.

"I hope with this information we can persuade member states to reconsider the decision to cancel the multinational force for eastern Zaire," Annan told reporters after talks with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.
He said the international community did not show sufficient political will to send the force created by a U.N. resolution in November but he would take the issue up on return to New York.
